name: Ikiki no Gomon (The Living Gate)

location.address: Oku-no-in (inner sanctuary) of Oyamazumi Shrine, Omishima, Imabari, Ehime Prefecture, Japan

access: Free, open year round, no set hours. A public path/steps has been built through the hollow root passage itself. About a 5-minute walk from Oyamazumi Shrine's main hall; no dedicated parking at the site (nearest is the free municipal Fuji Park lot).
transport: Omishima Island, reached by car via the Shimanami Kaido (Omishima IC, about 10 minutes to the shrine) or by bus from Imabari Station (approx. 65 minutes to the Oyamazumi Shrine stop, then a 5-minute walk).
verify_notes: Two independent sources (Japanese Wikipedia, citing the reference work 'Omishima wo chushin to suru Geiyo Soto-shi' and the on-site information board; and the City of Imabari's own tourism page) agree this is a genuinely singular destination: a huge old camphor whose split, hollowed root base forms a natural gate/tunnel (about 2m wide, 3m high, 7m long) that pilgrims historically walked through to reach Oyamazumi Shrine's inner sanctuary (Oku-no-in). The name 'Ikiki no Gomon' means roughly 'the gate of the living tree'. AGE DISPUTED, deliver as a range: the reference book gives 2,000 years, the on-site sign gives 3,000 years; neither is sourced to a scientific dating method, so treat as a loose estimate rather than a measured figure. GIRTH: main (larger) trunk circumference is given as 11m (recorded as girth_cm 1100). This is a double-trunked, multi-stemmed tree, not a single clean trunk: the combined circumference of the trunk union/stool is given as 15.5m (1550cm), and separately the circumference of the exposed ROOT MASS (not the trunk) at ground level is given as 32m (3200cm, and the City of Imabari page rounds this to 'approximately 30m' when describing the tree, which reads confusingly like a trunk figure but is the root spread). Do not repeat the 30-32m figure as a trunk measurement. HEALTH: originally a single-trunk camphor; the original main trunk is now largely dead/decaying, believers historically stripped its bark for use as a longevity charm which hastened its decline, and the tree nearly died in the Meiji era (late 19th century) but revived through vigorous new sprouting from the root base, which is now the healthy secondary trunk (4.5m/450cm circumference) carrying the tree today. This is one continuous living organism regenerating from its own root system, not a dead stump with unrelated saplings nearby (contrast with Wilson's Stump on Yakushima, which is dead and blocked). STATUS: designated an EHIME PREFECTURE Natural Monument on 1951-11-27. It is explicitly NOT part of the separate NATIONAL Natural Monument covering the wider grove of camphors ('Oyamazumi Shrine camphor grove') elsewhere on the shrine grounds; those are a different, ensemble-type designation and were not evaluated in this pass. COLLECTIBILITY: single named tree with one obvious place to stand (the gate itself); passes the 2026-08-31 single-famous-tree exception as a real Shimanami Kaido/Omishima tourist destination people travel to specifically (a well known 'power spot' on the cycling route), well outside any published city's day-trip radius (nearest published city is roughly 53km away). Recommend container new:Omishima (an island/place, not assumed to be a city, per the Kauai/Menorca/Madeira precedent).

name: Kawatana no Kusu no Mori (The Camphor Forest of Kawatana)

location.address: 6895 Kawatana-Shitaono, Toyoura-cho, Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi Prefecture, Japan

access: Free, publicly viewable. Reached in about 10 minutes by taxi/car from Kawatana Onsen Station (JR San-in Main Line), or about 20-30 minutes by car from the Chugoku Expressway (Kozuki IC or Shimonoseki IC). No fee or set hours found on the official tourism pages. Note the tree has been fenced/cordoned off around its base during its recovery (see health note below), so visitors view it from a short distance rather than approach the trunk closely.
transport: 10 minutes by taxi from Kawatana Onsen Station, JR San-in Main Line.
verify_notes: DESPITE THE NAME: 'Kusu no Mori' translates literally as 'camphor forest', but every source (Japanese Wikipedia, Yamaguchi Prefecture's own tourism site, Shimonoseki city sources) is explicit this is ONE SINGLE TREE, not a grove: 'one camphor tree growing so large it appears forest-like' (Wikipedia). The crown spans an enormous 58m east-west by 53m north-south (roughly 180m around the drip line) from 18 major limbs branching about 5m up the trunk, which is why it reads as a wood from a distance. Treated here as a single collectible point, not blocked as an ensemble, on that basis; this is the one candidate in this batch where the 'forest' in the name is misleading rather than descriptive. One of Japan's traditionally named 'Three Great Camphor Trees' (Nihon San Dai Shoju) and listed in the 'New Japan 100 Famous Trees'. National Natural Monument since 1922-10-12 (predates the postwar Cultural Properties Protection Law framework used elsewhere in this database, but functionally the same national designation). AGE: sources only give 'over 1,000 years' with no further precision or stated method; recorded as a floor (age_min 1000) rather than inventing an upper bound, per the vague-source rule. GIRTH: trunk circumference at breast/eye height (mokudoshi) is 11.2m = 1120cm; height 27m. HEALTH, the reason this is flagged: the tree began dying back suddenly in July 2017, losing most of its foliage, assessed by Shimonoseki city/Yamaguchi prefecture/the national Agency for Cultural Affairs at decline grade IV ('severely poor'), with roots largely rotted; the suspected but unconfirmed cause is oxygen-starved roots from fill dirt added during nearby park development. It was NOT dead: as of a 2023-06-21 local news piece and a Shimonoseki city report, new shoots and green leaves have been re-emerging from the trunk since around 2021-2022, described as tentative but real signs of recovery, and the city continues active vitality-restoration work with the prefecture and Agency for Cultural Affairs. Deliver as alive but declining/recovering, not as a healthy specimen; a photo request should specifically ask for a recent (2023 or later) dated image so the writer/photo pass does not accidentally use a pre-2017 photo showing a full green canopy that no longer exists. Historical legend: connected to Sengoku-era warlord Ouchi Yoshitaka, whose beloved horse 'Hibarige' is said to be buried nearby and enshrined as a horse deity, with an annual memorial on 28 March; good colour for the story. COLLECTIBILITY: single named tree, one obvious place to stand, passes the 2026-08-31 single-famous-tree exception (a National Natural Monument and one of Japan's 'three great camphors', a genuine specific-tree destination), well outside any published city's day-trip radius (nearest published city is roughly 83km away). Recommend container new:Kawatana.
